To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
low brain RAs protects against the development diastolic dysfunction, left ventricular hypertrophy and cardiac fibrosis in the aging heart.
low brain angiotensin protects against the development and progression of age-related diastsolic dysfunction and left cardiac remodeling.
low central Ang II protects against the development and progression of diastolic heart failure and improves body habitus in aging rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach for the treatment of age-related cardiovascular disease.
the effects of aging on the central renin–angitensin system (central RAS) and the role of the central RAS in meditating the effects of aging.
the role of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) in the development of age related diastolic dysfunction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
low brain Ang II is a novel, potentially important, and potentially therapeutic target for the treatment and prevention of diastolic heart failure in aging.
low brain RAs protects against the development and progression of age-related diostolic dysfunction, cardiac remodeling, and oxidative damage.
low glial brain RAS improves body habitus and diastolic cardiac function in aging male rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
low central RAS may have beneficial effects on the heart, and possibly other organs, during aging.
a reduction in the brain RAS, without affecting the peripheral RAS, may be a novel therapeutic target for the treatment of aging-related cardiac diastolic dysfunction.
low brain Ang II protects against the development and progression of cardiac aging and that this may be related, at least in part, to the maintenance of a healthy body mass.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain RAS may play an important role in the development of diastsolic dysfunction and body habitus in aging.
targeting the central RAS may be an effective strategy to prevent age-related diastole dysfunction.
the brain RAS may have a role in the development of cardiac diastolic dysfunction, and this could be related to effects of brain RAS on body habitus.
